title: Animal societies: how elephants, ants and wolves live and decide together

summary.text: Many animals live in groups that work together. A group like this is called a society. An elephant family is led by the oldest female, often a grandmother, because she remembers the most: where to find water in a dry year, and which dangers are real. An ant colony has a queen, but she does not give orders. Thousands of worker ants decide together, by leaving scent trails and following each other. A wolf pack is a family: a mother, a father and their young, who hunt together and raise the pups together. Humans are animals that live in societies too.
summary.art: Three panels side by side: an elephant family walking behind an old female at dusk, a line of ants carrying food along a kitchen platform, and a wolf family resting on a dry grassland.

intro.hook: Put one drop of sugar water near a line of ants and watch. One ant finds the drop. A few minutes later there are five, then twenty. Nobody can see an ant giving orders. So how does a crowd of ants agree where to go?
intro.text: Ants are not the only animals who act together. Elephants walk in families led by a grandmother. Wolves hunt as a family. In this unit you test how ants choose between two foods, and you find out who leads an elephant family and a wolf pack, and why. You also find out about a famous mistake scientists made about wolves.
intro.art: A child kneeling on a kitchen floor, watching a line of small black ants walk towards a drop of sugar water on a square of plastic.

outcomes: I can explain what an animal society is, and name three: an elephant family, an ant colony and a wolf pack.
I can explain why an elephant family follows the oldest female, the matriarch, and what she knows that younger elephants do not.
I can describe an ant colony: the queen, the workers and their jobs, and how ants share news of food with scent.
I can run a fair test with two sugar drops, count the ants over time, and explain how the colony chose without a leader.
I can explain that a wolf pack is a family, and why the old idea of a fighting 'alpha wolf' turned out to be wrong.
I can compare animal societies with human families and groups, using evidence, and say what scientists still argue about.

terms.meaning: A group of animals of one kind who live together and help each other, for a long time. Members of a society know each other.
terms.example: An elephant family, an ant colony and a wolf pack are all societies. So is a human village.
terms.art: A circle of different animal groups: elephants, ants, wolves and a human family.

terms.meaning: A group of large animals, such as elephants, cows or deer, who live and move together.
terms.example: A herd of elephants walks to the river every evening in the dry season.
terms.art: A herd of Asian elephants crossing a dry riverbed in a line.

terms.meaning: The female who leads a family. In elephants, she is usually the oldest female, and often the grandmother of the calves.
terms.example: When there is danger, the elephant family looks to the matriarch and gathers around her.
terms.art: An old female elephant with a torn ear at the front of her family, a calf behind her.

terms.meaning: A baby elephant. Cows, buffaloes, whales and giraffes also have calves.
terms.example: A newborn elephant calf walks under their mother's belly for shade.
terms.art: A small elephant calf standing in the shade under their mother.

terms.meaning: A large group of insects of one kind living together in one nest, such as ants, termites or honeybees.
terms.example: The ants in your kitchen probably all belong to one colony, with a nest inside a wall or under the floor.
terms.art: A cut-away drawing of an ant nest under the floor, with rooms full of ants, eggs and young.

terms.meaning: In an ant colony, the queen is the female who lays the eggs. She is usually the mother of all the other ants in the nest. She does not give orders.
terms.example: A queen ant may live for many years, laying eggs deep in the nest.
terms.art: A large queen ant in a nest room, surrounded by smaller worker ants and white eggs.

terms.meaning: A worker ant is a female ant who does the colony's jobs: looking after the young, cleaning, building, guarding and finding food. Worker ants do not lay the colony's eggs.
terms.example: The ants you see walking on the kitchen platform are workers, out looking for food.
terms.art: Worker ants doing different jobs: one carrying an egg, one digging, one carrying a crumb.

terms.meaning: To search for food. An ant who goes out to look for food is a forager.
terms.example: Crows forage in the rubbish bin. Ants forage along the kitchen floor.
terms.art: An ant walking along the edge of a steel plate, waving her feelers.

terms.meaning: A smell an animal makes to send a message to others of their kind. Ants use pheromones to mark a path to food and to warn of danger.
terms.example: An ant who finds sugar leaves a pheromone trail on her way home. Other ants smell it and follow it to the sugar.
terms.art: A dotted line of scent drawn behind an ant, with two more ants following the dots.

terms.meaning: The two feelers on an insect's head. Ants smell, taste and touch with their antennae. One feeler is called an antenna.
terms.example: When two ants meet on a path, they tap each other with their antennae.
terms.art: Two ants face to face, touching antennae.

terms.meaning: To bring more members to a job. An ant who finds food recruits other ants to help carry it.
terms.example: One ant found the jaggery and recruited twenty more within ten minutes.
terms.art: One ant leading a line of ants towards a lump of jaggery.

terms.meaning: A group of wolves or wild dogs who live and hunt together. A wolf pack is usually a family.
terms.example: An Indian wolf pack in the Deccan grasslands is usually a mother, a father and their young.
terms.art: A small family of Indian wolves trotting through dry grass.

terms.example: In a wolf pack, the older brothers and sisters bring food to the pups.
terms.art: Three wolf pups outside a den, an older young wolf bringing them food.

terms.meaning: To work together towards something that all of you need.
terms.example: Wolves cooperate when they hunt, and ants cooperate when they carry a big crumb together.
terms.art: Four ants together lifting a crumb much bigger than any one of them.

terms.meaning: The one others follow. A leader may know the way, start a move or keep the group together. A leader does not always give orders.
terms.example: In an elephant family the matriarch leads, because the others follow where she goes.
terms.art: An old elephant walking ahead, others following her footprints.

explanations.definition: An animal society is a group of animals of one kind who live together for a long time, know each other, and help each other to survive and raise their young.
explanations.description: A crowd of pigeons at a grain shop is not a society. The birds just happen to be in the same place. A society is different: its members stay together, know each other and share the work. Elephants, ants, wolves, honeybees, crows, monkeys and humans all live in societies. Humans are animals, and a human family or village is a society too. Living together has costs as well as gains. Members must share food and can pass on germs. But together they find food, stay safe and raise their young better than one animal alone.
examples: An elephant family walks together, eats together and protects the calves together.
An ant colony shares food: ants pass liquid food mouth to mouth to their sisters in the nest.
A street dog group in your neighbourhood may sleep in the same spot every night and chase off strange dogs together.
explanations.art: A pigeon crowd at a grain shop on one side, and an elephant family walking close together on the other, with a question mark between them.

explanations.concept: An elephant family is led by the oldest female
explanations.definition: An elephant family is a group of related females and their young: a grandmother, her daughters, her granddaughters and the small calves. The leader is called the matriarch. She is usually the oldest female.
explanations.description: Many people imagine that a big male with huge tusks leads the herd. He does not. Adult male elephants, called bulls, live alone or in loose groups of males. They visit families only for a short time. Young males leave their family as teenagers. So the family is a group of mothers, aunts, sisters and daughters. The family follows the matriarch. When she walks, they walk. When she stops to listen, they stop. When there is danger, they gather around her, with the calves in the middle. The scientist Cynthia Moss has studied the elephant families of Amboseli in Kenya since 1972, one of the longest studies of wild animals anywhere. In India, Asian elephant families live the same way. Female Asian elephants have no tusks, or only tiny ones.
examples: In the dry season, elephant families in Nagarhole and Bandipur in Karnataka walk to the Kabini river. Hundreds of elephants gather along its banks.
When a calf squeals, the females nearby rush to them and rumble softly.
A teenage male elephant starts to wander away from his family, and after a while lives on his own.
explanations.art: An Asian elephant family walking in a line through a forest: an old female at the front, younger females, and two small calves in the middle.

explanations.description: An old matriarch has lived through more dry years, more floods and more dangers than anyone else in her family. Scientists think her family follows her because her memory keeps them alive. Karen McComb and her team played recordings of lions roaring to elephant families in Amboseli. Families with an old matriarch reacted most strongly to the roar of male lions, who are the most dangerous to calves. Families with a younger matriarch often reacted less to them. In a bad drought in Tanzania in 1993, some families walked far out of the park to find water, and they lost fewer calves. The scientists think their old matriarchs remembered a drought from about 35 years before. Not everyone agrees on how much one leader decides. Some studies show that other females can start a move too.
examples: An old matriarch may remember a water pool that no younger elephant has ever seen.
Elephants can tell the calls of their friends from the calls of strangers. Families with old matriarchs are better at it.
Families who lose their old matriarch to poachers often show more signs of stress for years afterwards.

perspectives.who: Karen McComb and Cynthia Moss, elephant scientists
perspectives.explanation: The matriarch matters most. Her age and memory are the family's store of knowledge. Families with old matriarchs make better choices about danger.
The matriarch often leads, but other experienced females also start moves and help decide. The family decides together more than one leader does.

perspectives.who: T. N. C. Vidya and her team, who study Asian elephants at Kabini in Karnataka
perspectives.explanation: Asian elephant families there often split into small groups and join up again. So what is true in Africa may not be exactly true in India. We need to study each kind of elephant.

explanations.art: An old elephant with a trunk raised, listening, while her family waits behind her.

explanations.concept: An ant colony: a queen and her worker daughters
explanations.definition: An ant colony is a family of ants living in one nest. A queen lays the eggs. Almost all the other ants are her daughters, the workers, who do all the other jobs.
explanations.description: Every worker ant you have ever seen is a female. Male ants hatch only at certain times of year. They have wings and fly out to mate, and they live only a short time. The queen stays deep in the nest and lays eggs. Workers look after the eggs and young, clean the nest, build, guard and bring in food. In many kinds of ants, the young workers work inside the nest. Older workers go out to forage. So the ants you see in your kitchen are probably older workers. The queen gives the workers no orders. Each worker senses what is going on around her and decides what to do next.
examples: The tiny ants on your kitchen platform belong to a nest you may never see, inside a wall or under a tile.
Weaver ants, common in Kerala, Odisha and the Northeast, build nests in trees by pulling leaves together. They glue the leaves with silk from their young.
Termites live in colonies too, but a termite colony has a king as well as a queen.
explanations.art: A cut-away of an ant nest: the queen in a deep room, young workers carrying eggs nearby, older workers walking out of the entrance.

explanations.concept: How ants share news of food
explanations.definition: An ant who finds food leaves a scent trail, made of pheromone, on her way back to the nest. Other ants follow the trail to the food, and add their own scent on the way back.
explanations.description: The first ant to find food is often alone. She drinks or picks up a piece, and walks home, dabbing the floor with pheromone from her body. In the nest she meets her sisters and passes them some food. They follow her trail out. When they find the food, they lay scent on the way home too. So the trail gets stronger, and more ants follow it. When the food runs out, ants stop laying scent. The smell fades after a while, and the ants stop coming. In lab tests with black garden ants, ants that found sweeter sugar laid more scent. So a sweet food builds a strong trail quickly.
examples: A dropped piece of laddu can have a line of ants within half an hour.
If you wipe a short piece of the ant road with a wet cloth, the ants arriving there stop and wander, because the scent is gone.
Ants passing each other on a trail tap antennae. They smell where the other ant has been.
explanations.art: A line of ants between a crack in the wall and a piece of laddu, with faint dotted scent marks on the floor.

explanations.concept: How a colony decides without a leader
explanations.definition: A colony makes choices as a group. Each ant makes small choices, such as which trail to follow and how much scent to lay. Together, these small choices become one choice for the whole colony.
explanations.description: Think of your sugar test. No ant tasted every drop and then gave orders. The ants that drank the strong sugar laid more scent on the way home. More ants followed that trail, so more ants laid scent there. The trail to the weak drop stayed faint. Soon most ants were at the strong drop. The scientist Deborah Gordon studied harvester ants in the deserts of Arizona for more than 30 years. She found that ants decide whether to go out for food by how often they meet ants coming back with food. Many quick meetings mean food is easy to find. Scientists call a group choice like this collective decision-making. Sometimes the crowd gets stuck. If ants find a weak drop first and build a strong trail, they may keep going there even after a sweeter drop appears.
examples: Honeybees choose a new home the same way: scouts dance for the places they found, and the best place gets the most dancers.
A flock of starlings turns together because each bird watches the seven or so birds nearest to them.
People on a busy railway platform make paths through the crowd without anyone in charge.
explanations.art: Two drops of sugar water, one crowded with ants and one with just two, and thick and thin scent trails leading to each.

explanations.description: Each ant senses, remembers and chooses. A colony also seems to choose, as a whole, in ways no single ant could. Some scientists call a colony a superorganism. This means a group that works like one body, with each ant like a cell. Others say that is only a way of speaking. Scientists still argue about it.
examples: Army ants link their own bodies into living bridges across gaps, so the rest of the colony can cross.
A colony moves house when the old nest floods, with workers carrying the eggs and young to safety.
Your body is made of billions of cells, and each cell senses and responds too.

perspectives.who: Scientists who use the word superorganism
perspectives.explanation: The colony is one living whole. The workers are like the cells of a body and the queen is like its egg-making organ. The colony thinks and chooses as one.
A colony is many ants, each following simple rules. Calling it one mind is a useful picture, but the choosing is done by the ants.
Both are true at once. Each ant has her own small mind, and the colony has a larger one made of them.

explanations.art: A drawing of an ant colony shaped like one big ant, made of thousands of small ants.

explanations.concept: A wolf pack is a family
explanations.definition: A wild wolf pack is usually a family: a mother and a father and their young from the last one to three years.
explanations.description: The parents lead the pack. They choose where to travel and start the hunt. The young wolves follow them, as children follow their parents. Older young wolves help to feed and guard the new pups. Wolves bring meat back to the den in their stomachs and bring it up again for the pups to eat. When young wolves grow up, most of them leave to find a mate and start their own pack. Wolves howl to find each other when they are apart, and to warn other packs to keep away. Indian wolves live in the dry grasslands and farmland of the Deccan, Gujarat and Rajasthan. Their packs are small.
examples: In Velavadar National Park in Gujarat, wolf packs hunt blackbuck in the grasslands.
A wolf alone can rarely catch a large deer. A pack hunting together often can.
Street dogs in Indian cities are related to wolves. They often live in small groups too.
explanations.art: A wolf mother and father lying on a rock, three young wolves playing below, and two pups at the den.

explanations.description: Humans are animals who live in societies: families, villages, schools and cities. Like elephants, we learn a lot from older people. The scientist Kristen Hawkes studied the Hadza people in Tanzania. She found that grandmothers there gather food that helps their grandchildren grow. She suggested that grandmothers helped humans survive for thousands of years. This idea is called the grandmother hypothesis. Lauren Brent and her team found something like it in killer whales. Old females who no longer have calves lead their families to salmon, especially in years with little food. Scientists still argue about how much grandmothers explain.
examples: A grandmother who remembers which leaves are safe to eat, and which plants help a fever.
Older killer whale females swim in front when food is hard to find.
In many Indian homes, children learn recipes, songs and festival customs from their grandmothers.
explanations.art: A grandmother teaching a girl to sort tamarind on a veranda, with an elephant matriarch and calf drawn faintly in the clouds behind them.

agreed.text: Elephant families are groups of related females and their young, usually led by the oldest female. Adult males live apart.
agreed.evidence: Scientists in Kenya have watched and named the same elephant families for over 50 years. Studies in India and Sri Lanka find the same: related females stay together.

agreed.text: Old matriarchs know more about dangers than young ones, and their families do better.
agreed.evidence: In playback tests, families with old matriarchs reacted more wisely to lion roars and to the calls of strange elephants.

agreed.text: Worker ants are all females. The queen lays the eggs but does not give orders.
agreed.evidence: Scientists have watched ant colonies closely for many years. They have not found any ant giving orders. Each worker reacts to what she smells and meets.

agreed.text: Ants lay pheromone trails to food, and other ants follow them.
agreed.evidence: Scientists can collect the scent from an ant's body and draw a line with the scent on paper. Ants follow the line even with no food at the end.

agreed.text: A wild wolf pack is usually a family led by the parents.
agreed.evidence: Years of watching wild wolves, and testing their genes, show that most pack members are parents and their young.

challenging.claim: A wolf pack is ruled by an 'alpha' wolf who fought his way to the top.
challenging.who: A very common idea from older books, films and dog training
challenging.for: Wolves put together as strangers in zoos did fight for rank.
challenging.against: Wild packs are families, and the 'alpha' pair are simply the parents. The scientist who spread the word, David Mech, later showed it was wrong for wild wolves.
challenging.context: This card is about one of the most famous mistakes about animal societies.

challenging.claim: The queen ant rules the colony and tells the workers what to do.
challenging.who: Many people, because of the word 'queen'
challenging.for: The queen is the biggest ant and the mother of the others, and the workers feed and protect her.
challenging.against: The queen gives no orders. Each worker decides what to do from what she senses around her.
challenging.context: Does the queen ant rule? This card looks at what her name makes people expect.

challenging.claim: The biggest male elephant leads the herd.
challenging.for: Bull elephants are the largest and strongest, with the biggest tusks.
challenging.against: Adult bulls live apart from the families. Families are led by an old female, the matriarch, who has the most experience.
challenging.context: Who leads an elephant herd? This card looks at a common guess.

challenging.claim: Every insect queen keeps her place by bullying the others.
challenging.who: An old idea about insect societies
challenging.for: In some wasps, the queen does bully the others.
challenging.against: Raghavendra Gadagkar and his team at the Indian Institute of Science in Bengaluru studied a paper wasp common across India, Ropalidia marginata. The queen there is calm and meek. When she is taken away, one worker becomes very aggressive for a while, and then becomes the next calm queen.
challenging.context: This card is about an Indian discovery that a queen can lead without bullying.

challenging.claim: An ant colony is one mind, a superorganism.
challenging.for: The colony makes good group choices that no single ant makes, such as picking the sweeter food or the best new nest.
challenging.against: Others say the choosing is done by many ants, each following simple rules, and 'one mind' is only a picture.
challenging.context: Is a colony one being, or many? This card looks at both sides.

challenging.claim: Grandmothers helped humans survive, the way matriarchs help elephants.
challenging.for: Hadza grandmothers in Tanzania gather food that helps their grandchildren grow. Killer whale grandmothers lead their families to food.
challenging.against: Other scientists think fathers, older children and the whole group mattered as much. It is hard to test what happened long ago.
challenging.context: Do grandmothers matter for humans as they do for elephants? This card looks at an idea that is still argued about.

big_questions.q: Your ants chose the sweeter drop together. Who made the choice: each ant, the whole colony, or both?
big_questions.hint: Think about what one ant did, and what the crowd did. Could one ant alone have done what the crowd did?

big_questions.q: An old matriarch remembers a water pool from 35 years ago. Where is a family's knowledge kept, if not in a book?
big_questions.hint: Think of what an older relative or neighbour knows that nobody wrote down.

big_questions.q: Why do some animals live alone, like a tiger, and others in groups, like elephants?
big_questions.hint: Think about food. Is a tiger's food easy to share? Is an elephant's?

big_questions.q: Every worker ant is a female, and elephant families are led by females. Why do people so often picture a male leader?
big_questions.hint: Think about stories, cartoons and words like 'king of the jungle'. Where do our pictures come from?

big_questions.q: Is a city like an ant colony? Who decides where people walk on a crowded street?
big_questions.hint: Watch a busy road or a market from a balcony. Does anyone give orders?

big_questions.q: If you grew up with no one older to learn from, what would you not know?
big_questions.hint: Think of a young elephant whose matriarch was killed. What would she have to work out alone?

story.title: The Grandmother Who Knew the Way
story.note: Asian elephant families led by an old female, bulls living apart, and the summer gathering of elephants along the Kabini river at the edge of Nagarhole are real. Nila, Ravi, Kempamma, the elephant called Doddamma and this summer are made up.
text: Nila lived in a small village at the edge of the Nagarhole forest in Karnataka. Behind her house was a field of ragi, and behind the field was the forest. In the evenings, elephants sometimes walked along the edge of the trees.
That April, her cousin Ravi came from Bengaluru for the holidays. Ravi was ten, two years older than Nila. He knew a great deal about cars and nothing at all about elephants.
It was the hottest summer anyone could remember. The small pools in the forest had dried into cracked mud. The grass was brown. Even the stream near the village was only a line of wet sand.
"The elephants will come past soon," said Nila's grandmother, Kempamma. "When the forest dries, they walk to the river."
Kempamma had lived by the forest all her life. For many years she had cooked for the forest guards at the watchtower. She knew every path, and she knew the elephants who used them.
"Will the big tusker lead them?" asked Ravi. "The one with the giant tusks?"
Nila laughed. "Wait and see," she said.

That evening the three of them climbed onto the flat roof of the house. Kempamma brought a torch, but she did not switch it on. "We watch from far away," she said. "And we keep quiet. An elephant is a big, strong person, and she has a calf to protect."
Just as the sky turned orange, the leaves at the edge of the forest moved. A grey head came out of the trees. Then a second, and a third.
The first elephant was old. Her skin hung in loose folds, and one of her ears had a torn edge, like a leaf a goat had nibbled. She had no tusks at all.
"That's Doddamma," Nila whispered. "It means big mother. She's the oldest in her family."
"But where's the tusker?" Ravi whispered back.
"Not here," said Kempamma. "The grown-up males live on their own. This family is all mothers and daughters and little ones. Look."

Ravi counted. Behind Doddamma came two big females, then three smaller ones. Two tiny calves walked right under their mothers' bellies, in the shade. At the very end walked a young male with short new tusks. He kept stopping to pull at branches, then hurrying to catch up.
"He's a teenager," said Kempamma. "In a year or two he will wander off and live with other males. That is how it is with elephants. The daughters stay. The sons go."

At the dry stream, Doddamma stopped. The whole family stopped behind her. She lifted her trunk and held it in the air, turning it slowly, smelling the wind. Then she began to dig in the sand with her front foot, and with the tip of her trunk.
"What's she doing?" asked Ravi.
"Watch," said Nila.

After a while, the hole in the sand turned dark. Water was seeping into it from below. Doddamma drank first, sucking the water into her trunk and squirting it into her mouth. Then she stepped back, and a mother pushed her calf forward to drink.
"How did she know the water was there?" Ravi asked.

"She has done it before," said Kempamma. "Many times. Doddamma is older than your father, Ravi. She has lived through more dry summers than anyone in her family. The young mothers don't know where the hidden water is. She does."

There was not enough water in the hole for everyone. After a while Doddamma rumbled, a deep sound that Ravi felt in his chest more than heard. She turned away from the stream and set off down the long path towards the river. One by one, the family followed her.
"Why not stay and dig more?" said Ravi.

Kempamma was quiet for a moment. "Many years ago, when I was a young woman, the rains failed for two years," she said. "Even the streams dried to dust. The herds that stayed in the forest suffered. One old female led her family all the way to the river, many hours' walk. Her family lived. I think that old female was Doddamma's mother. And Doddamma walked behind her, as a young elephant, and learned the way."
Nila looked at her grandmother. "So Doddamma remembers what her own mother showed her."
"And her daughters will remember what she shows them," said Kempamma.
Ravi was quiet for a long time. "I thought the strongest one would be the leader," he said at last.
"The strongest one can push a tree over," said Nila. "But pushing a tree over doesn't find you water. The one who knows the way is the one they follow."

A week later, Kempamma took them both on the forest department's bus along the Kabini river. The water had shrunk back, leaving wide green grass along the banks. On the grass were elephants. Not one family, but dozens of families, hundreds of elephants, grazing and drinking and spraying mud over their backs.
Ravi pressed his face to the window. Then he grabbed Nila's arm.
"Look! The torn ear!"
At the edge of the water, an old female was spraying water over a calf. Her ear had a torn edge, like a leaf a goat had nibbled.
Doddamma had brought her family to the river again.
story.epiphany: For the parent: an elephant family follows the oldest female, the matriarch, because she has the most experience. Doddamma found water under the dry sand because she had done it in earlier dry summers. When there was not enough, she led her family to the river, a path she learned as a young elephant from her own mother. Knowledge passes down a family of females, from grandmother to mother to daughter. The young male will leave, as male elephants do. Size and strength did not decide who led. Memory did. Kempamma, who has watched the forest all her life, plays the same part for Nila and Ravi.
ask: Ravi expected the big tusker to lead the herd. Why was he not with the family at all?
How did Doddamma find water in a dry stream?
Why did the family follow Doddamma, and not the biggest or youngest female?
Where did Doddamma learn the way to the river?
Kempamma knew things about the forest that Ravi did not. Who in your family knows things nobody else knows?

games.title: Herd, Colony or Pack?
games.context: This is a card game about three animal societies. You read a clue and say whether it is about an elephant family, an ant colony, a wolf pack, or all three.

rules: Cut out the 18 cards. Shuffle them and put them in a pile, clue side up.
On your turn, read the top clue aloud. Say which society it is about: elephant family, ant colony, wolf pack, or all three.
Turn the card over. If you were right, keep the card and put it on the matching space of the mat. If you were wrong, put it at the bottom of the pile.
Before the next player's turn, say one more fact about the society on the card, if you can. A good fact wins you a second turn.
When the pile is empty, the player with the most cards wins. Playing alone, try to win all 18 cards in as few turns as you can.

flow.do: 1. Cut out the cards and lay out the mat. 2. Shuffle the cards into a pile, clue side up.
flow.say: Each card has a clue about elephants, ants or wolves. Some clues fit all three. Let's see if you can tell them apart.
flow.kid: Shuffle the cards. Put them in a pile. Read the top card.
flow.context: This is the first step of Herd, Colony or Pack. Here you set up the cards.

flow.do: Take turns reading a card, saying the answer and turning it over.
flow.say: Read the clue. Which society is it? Turn it over and check.
flow.kid: Read the clue. Say elephant, ant, wolf or all three. Turn it over. Were you right?

check.q: Which society is led by a mother and a father who are the parents of the others?
check.why: A wild wolf pack is usually a family, and the parents lead. An elephant family is led by the oldest female. An ant colony has a queen, but no ant leads.

flow.do: Count the cards and look at the 'All three' pile together.
flow.say: Look at the 'All three' cards. What do all three societies share?
flow.kid: Look at the 'All three' cards. What do all three share?

ask.q: What do elephant families, ant colonies and wolf packs all have in common?
good: They are all families.
The young learn from older members.
They help each other survive.

games.title: The Dry Season Walk
games.context: This is a board game about elephant families walking through a dry forest to the river. Players answer questions about elephant families to reach the Kabini river first.

setup.art: A winding forest path board of 17 squares, numbered 0 to 16, from a dry forest to a blue river, with paper elephant counters on square 0.
setup.caption: 1. Put every elephant family counter on square 0.

setup.art: A player answering a question card, then rolling a dice and moving a counter along the path.
setup.caption: 2. Answer a card, roll and move towards the river.

printables.title: A forest path board with 17 squares, numbered 0 to 16, from the dry forest to the Kabini river
items: Square 0: The dry forest. Start here.
Square 3: DRY POOL: the pool is mud. Go back 2 squares, unless you can say how an old matriarch finds water.
Square 5: DANGER NEAR: say what an elephant family does when they sense danger. Then move on 1 square.
Square 7: TEENAGE BULL: your young male wanders off to live with other males. Say why he leaves, then move on 1.

printables.title: 16 question cards to cut out (the answer is on the back)

items.f: Who leads an elephant family?
items.b: The matriarch, usually the oldest female

items.f: Why does the family follow the oldest female?
items.b: She remembers the most: water, paths and dangers

items.f: Where do adult male elephants live?
items.b: Alone, or in loose groups of males

items.f: What is a baby elephant called?
Do female Asian elephants have big tusks?
items.b: No. They have none, or tiny ones

items.f: How does an elephant find water in a dry riverbed?
items.b: She digs in the sand with her foot and trunk

items.f: In Africa, which lions are most dangerous to elephant calves: males or females?
Name one way elephants talk to each other.
Who stays in the family for life: daughters or sons?
Where do many elephant families gather in summer, in Karnataka?
Who does an elephant calf learn the way from?
What happens when a family hears danger?
items.b: They gather round, with the calves in the middle

items.f: Who leads the family when the matriarch dies?
items.b: Usually one of the older females

items.f: Is the biggest elephant always the leader?
items.b: No. The most experienced female leads

items.f: TELL IT: say one thing an older person you know remembers that you do not.
items.b: Any true answer wins the move

items.f: TELL IT: in one sentence, say why old age helps a leader.

rules: You need the board, the cards, one dice and a counter for each player. Each counter is an elephant family. Put every counter on square 0.
On your turn, another player reads you the top question card. Playing alone? Read it yourself, say your answer, then turn the card over to check.
Answer right, and roll the dice and move that many squares. Answer wrong, and move 1 square.
If you land on a square with a message, do what it says. Squares you are sent to by a message do nothing more.
On a TELL IT card, any sensible true answer counts as right.
When the cards run out, shuffle them and use them again.
The first family to reach the Kabini river, square 16, wins. You don't need the exact number to finish.

flow.do: 1. Lay out the board. 2. Put each counter on square 0. 3. Shuffle the question cards and put them face down.
flow.say: It is the hottest month. The forest pools have dried. Each of us leads an elephant family to the river. Answer questions to move.
flow.kid: Put your family on square 0. Mix the cards. Can you lead your family to the river?
flow.context: This is the first step of The Dry Season Walk. It is a board game about leading an elephant family to water.

flow.do: Take turns. Read a card, answer, check, roll and move.
flow.say: Read your card. Answer it. If you're right, roll and move.
flow.kid: Answer your card. Right? Roll the dice and move. Wrong? Move 1.

check.q: You land on DRY POOL. What can an old matriarch do to find water?
options: Dig in a dry riverbed where she found water before
check.why: An old matriarch remembers where water was in earlier dry years. In a dry riverbed she digs, and water seeps into the hole from the sand below. Waiting for rain could take weeks. The youngest calf has never seen a dry year.

flow.do: When someone reaches the river, talk about the game.
flow.say: Which squares sent families back? What did the matriarch's memory help with?
flow.kid: Which squares were hard? How did the old matriarch help?

experiments.title: Weak Sugar or Strong Sugar: which drop does the colony choose?
experiments.context: In this experiment you put a weak sugar drop and a strong sugar drop near an ant road. You count the ants at each drop every 5 minutes, to see how the colony chooses.
experiments.question: If ants find a weak sugar drop and a strong sugar drop at the same time, will the colony end up at one of them? Which one, and how?
experiments.predict: Guess first. After half an hour, will there be more ants at the weak drop, more at the strong drop, or the same at both? Why do you think so?
experiments.fair_test: Change only how sweet the drops are. Use the same amount of each drop, the same kind of square, the same distance from the ant road, and put both down at the same moment. Count both drops at the same time. If you have time, do it again the next day with the two squares swapped, because one side might be nearer the nest.

materials.item: sugar
water
two small steel cups or katoris, and a teaspoon
two squares about 5 cm across, cut from a clean, dry milk packet or from aluminium foil
a pen to write W and S on the squares
a clock or a phone timer
a magnifying glass, if you have one
a damp cloth, for cleaning up

schedule.what: Find an ant road. Put down a weak and a strong sugar drop. Count the ants on each every 5 minutes for 30 minutes.

experiments.record: Fill in the table every 5 minutes. Then draw two bars for the last count: one for the weak drop and one for the strong drop.

setup.art: A line of small ants walking along the edge of a kitchen platform, with two plastic squares marked W and S placed a hand's width to one side.
setup.caption: 1. Find an ant road. Put the two squares a hand's width from it, side by side.

setup.art: Two steel katoris, one with a few grains of sugar in water labelled W, one with thick sugar water labelled S, and a teaspoon.
setup.caption: 2. Mix a weak drop and a strong drop.

setup.art: A child sitting still beside the squares, counting ants with a finger in the air, a phone timer showing 15 minutes.
setup.caption: 3. Count the ants on each square every 5 minutes.

flow.do: 1. Look for ants along the kitchen platform, the window sill or near the dustbin. 2. Watch which way they walk for one minute. 3. Put the two squares in a line along the ant road, each a hand's width from the road, about 15 cm apart.
flow.say: First we need to find the ants' road. Let's watch where they walk, without touching them. We'll put both squares the same distance from the road.
flow.kid: Find a line of ants. Watch where they walk. Put both squares near the line. Keep them the same distance away.
flow.parent: If you can't find ants, leave a few grains of sugar on the kitchen platform for an hour first, then look. Ants are often busiest in the evening.
flow.context: This is the first step of the sugar drop test. Here you find where the ants walk and set out two squares.

flow.do: 1. Write W on one square and S on the other. 2. In the first cup, mix 2 teaspoons of water with one pinch of sugar. This is the weak mix, W. 3. In the second cup, mix 2 teaspoons of water with 2 teaspoons of sugar. This is the strong mix, S. Stir each for one minute. 4. Put half a teaspoon of each mix on its square, at the same moment. 5. Start the timer.
flow.say: W is weak, with just a pinch of sugar. S is strong, very sweet. Before we put them down, tell me your guess. After half an hour, where will most ants be? Why do you think so?
flow.kid: Mix the weak cup and the strong cup. Put a drop on each square. Start the timer. Now guess. Where will most ants be? Why?

ask.q: Where do you think most ants will be after half an hour, and why?
good: At the strong drop, because ants like sweeter food.
The same at both, because ants can't tell from far away.
At whichever drop they find first, because they will follow the first trail.

flow.parent: Accept any guess with a reason. Don't hint. The strong mix will look thick and may not all dissolve. That is fine.
flow.context: This step of the sugar drop test is where you mix the weak and strong drops and make your guess.

flow.do: 1. Every 5 minutes, count the ants on each square and write both numbers in the table. 2. In between, sit still and watch. 3. Follow one ant from the strong drop with your eyes. Does she walk straight back towards the ant road?
flow.say: We count both squares at the same time, every 5 minutes. In between, let's watch what the ants do. Do they meet each other?
flow.kid: Every 5 minutes, count the ants on each square. Write the numbers down. In between, watch one ant. Where does she go?

ask.q: What do two ants do when they meet on the path?
good: They touch each other with their antennae.
They stop for a moment, then walk on.

flow.parent: Ants that keep moving are hard to count. Count the ants touching the square, and count twice if you are unsure. If after 15 minutes no ant has come to either drop, move both squares closer to the ant road, together, and start the count again. Sometimes the ants find the weak drop first and keep crowding it. That is a real result too, and the explanation cards say why it happens.
flow.think: No ant has tasted both drops and told the others. So how do the ants end up at one more than the other?

flow.do: 1. Look at your table together. 2. Ask your child to say what they found, what they saw, and why they think it happened.
flow.say: Let's look at the numbers. What did you find? What did you see that tells you so? Why do you think it happened?
flow.kid: Look at your numbers. Which drop has more ants? How did the number change? Why do you think so?

check.q: Suppose most ants ended up at the strong drop. How did the colony make this choice?
options: The queen came out and sent the ants there
Ants that drank the strong sugar laid more scent, so more ants followed their trail
Every ant tasted both drops and picked the best one
check.why: Ants that find very sweet food lay more pheromone on their way home. More ants follow the stronger trail, and they lay scent too, so the crowd grows fast. The queen stays deep in the nest and gives no orders. Picking 'every ant tasted both drops' is a good guess, but most ants only ever visit one drop. The colony chose because many ants each made a small choice.

flow.parent: Let your child explain before you read the explanation cards. If the weak drop won, ask which drop the ants found first.

flow.do: Wait for the ants to finish, or wipe the squares and floor with a damp cloth so the ants go home. Don't spray or squash them.
flow.say: The ants did our experiment with us. Let's clean up gently and let them go home.
flow.kid: Wipe up the sugar with a damp cloth. Let the ants go home.

experiments.title: Ask the Elders: who remembers the most about our place?
experiments.context: Elephant families follow the oldest female, because she remembers the most. In this experiment you ask people of different ages in your family the same questions, to see who knows most about your place.
experiments.question: Do older people in our family know more about the place where we live, or does it depend on the question?
experiments.predict: Guess first. Who will answer the most questions: you, a grown-up, or the oldest person you ask? Why do you think so?
experiments.fair_test: Ask everyone the same 6 questions, in the same order, with no hints. Nobody hears anyone else's answers. Give 1 point for each full answer.

materials.item: a notebook and a pencil
a phone, to call a grandparent or an older neighbour if they don't live with you

schedule.what: Write 6 questions. Ask three people of different ages, and score their answers.

experiments.record: Fill in the table. Draw a bar for each person's total.

setup.art: A child writing six questions in a notebook, three under 'long ago' and three under 'now'.
setup.caption: 1. Write 3 questions about long ago and 3 about now.

setup.art: A child asking a grandmother questions on a phone video call, notebook open.
setup.caption: 2. Ask each person the same questions, with no hints.

setup.art: A notebook page with three bars of different heights, labelled with names and ages.
setup.caption: 3. Score the answers and compare.

flow.do: 1. Write 3 questions about long ago, for example: 'Where did people here get water before there were taps?' 2. Write 3 questions about now, for example: 'Which bus goes to the nearest market?' 3. Check that each question has a clear answer that another person could confirm.
flow.say: An elephant matriarch remembers where water was in dry years long ago. Let's see what the people in our family remember. We need questions about long ago and questions about now.
flow.kid: Write 3 questions about long ago. Write 3 questions about now. Make sure each has a clear answer.
flow.parent: Other good questions: 'Which month do the first heavy rains usually come here?', 'What did this area look like before our building was built?', 'Where is the nearest medical shop open at night?', 'What is the name of the newest shop on our road?'.

flow.do: Choose three people: your child, a grown-up, and the oldest person you can reach. Ask your child to guess who will score most, and why.
flow.say: Who do you think will answer the most questions? Why do you think so?
flow.kid: Who will answer the most? Make a guess. Say why.

ask.q: Who will score most, and why?
good: Grandmother, because she has lived here longest.
Me, because I know the new shops.
It depends on the question.

flow.do: 1. Ask each person the 6 questions, one at a time, in the same order. 2. Don't give hints. 3. Write down each answer. 4. Answer the questions yourself first, before anyone else, so you don't hear their answers.
flow.say: We ask everyone exactly the same way, so the test is fair. No hints, even if they get stuck.
flow.kid: Answer the questions yourself first. Then ask the others. Same questions, same order. No hints!
flow.parent: A grown-up helps to make the phone call. Older people may want to tell long stories. Listen, and write down the answer to the question.

flow.do: 1. Give 1 point for each full answer. 2. Add up the 'long ago' and 'now' points for each person. 3. Draw a bar for each person's total.
flow.say: Let's score them. Who knew most about long ago? Who knew most about now? What does that tell us?
flow.kid: Give 1 point for each good answer. Add them up. Draw a bar for each person.

check.q: In a test like this, the grandmother scored 3 out of 3 on 'long ago' questions, and the child scored 3 out of 3 on 'now' questions. What does this show?
options: What a person knows depends on what they have lived through
check.why: People know most about what they have lived through. A grandmother remembers years nobody else in the family saw. A child knows the newest shops. That is why an old matriarch is so useful in a drought: she lived through droughts long ago. Picking 'older people always know more' misses the 'now' questions, where the child did best.

activities.title: Who Is in Charge? Watch an ant road for five minutes
activities.context: This is a short first look at ants. You watch a line of ants and look for a boss.

materials.item: a line of ants in your home, on a wall, a sill or the kitchen platform
a magnifying glass, if you have one

schedule.what: Watch a line of ants. Look for a boss. Watch what ants do when they meet.

activities.record: Write one thing you noticed and one thing you wonder.

setup.art: A child crouching by a wall, holding a magnifying glass over a line of ants.
setup.caption: 1. Find a line of ants and watch quietly.

setup.art: A close-up of two ants on a path touching antennae.
setup.caption: 2. Watch what two ants do when they meet.

flow.do: 1. Find a line of ants. 2. Pick one ant and follow her with your finger in the air above her, without touching. 3. Count how many other ants she meets in one minute.
flow.say: Let's pick one ant and follow her for one minute. How many other ants does she meet? What does she do when she meets one?
flow.kid: Pick one ant. Follow her with your finger in the air. Don't touch her. How many ants does she meet?
flow.context: This is the first step of the ant road watch. You follow one ant and count who she meets.
flow.parent: If you cannot find ants, put a few grains of sugar on a plate on the kitchen platform for an hour, then look again.

flow.do: Watch the whole line for two minutes. Look for any ant who seems to be the boss.
flow.say: Is there a boss ant telling the others where to go? What makes you think so?
flow.kid: Look at the whole line. Is there a boss ant? What makes you think so?

ask.q: Did you see a boss ant?
good: No. They all seem to be doing the same thing.
No, but they touch each other when they meet.

flow.parent: Most children expect a leader. Don't correct them now. The sugar drop test lets them find out.

flow.do: Leave your child with a question.
flow.say: So if nobody is the boss, how do all these ants know where to go?
flow.kid: No boss. But they all go the same way. How do they know?
flow.think: How could thousands of ants agree on where to go, if nobody gives orders?

activities.title: Draw an Elephant Family Tree
activities.context: In this activity you draw the family tree of one elephant family, to see who stays, who leaves and who leads.

materials.item: a large sheet of paper and coloured pencils

schedule.what: Draw a made-up elephant family tree from the clues, then mark who leads and who will leave.

activities.record: Your family tree, with the matriarch circled and the young males marked with an arrow pointing away.

setup.art: A family tree drawn on paper: one old elephant at the top, three daughters below, small calves below them.
setup.caption: 1. Draw the grandmother at the top and her daughters below.

setup.art: The same tree with a circle around the grandmother and an arrow from a young male pointing off the page.
setup.caption: 2. Circle the leader. Draw an arrow for each young male who will leave.

flow.do: Read the clues aloud, one at a time, and draw as you go. Clue 1: The grandmother is 58. She is the oldest. Clue 2: She has three daughters, aged 35, 30 and 22. Clue 3: The 35-year-old has a daughter of 12 and a son of 14. Clue 4: The 30-year-old has a baby daughter of 1. Clue 5: The 22-year-old has a son of 3.
flow.say: This is a made-up elephant family, but the family is built the way real ones are. Draw the grandmother at the top. Then draw her daughters, then their children.
flow.kid: Draw the grandmother at the top. She is 58. Draw her three daughters below her. Then draw their calves.
flow.context: This is the first step of the elephant family tree. You draw a made-up family from clues.

flow.do: 1. Circle the leader. 2. Draw an arrow away from each male who will leave as a teenager. 3. Count the females and count the males.
flow.say: Who leads this family? Which elephants will leave in a few years? Who will stay?
flow.kid: Circle the leader. Draw an arrow for each boy who will leave. Who stays?

check.q: In this family, who will most likely leave in the next few years?
options: The grandmother, because she is old
check.why: Young male elephants leave their family as teenagers and live alone or with other males. Daughters stay with their mothers and grandmother all their lives. Picking the 12-year-old daughter is a natural guess, but female elephants stay.

flow.do: Ask who would lead if the grandmother died.
flow.say: If the grandmother died, who do you think would lead the family? Why?
flow.kid: If the grandmother died, who would lead? Why?

good: The 35-year-old, because she is the next oldest and knows the most.
One of the older daughters.

activities.title: Jobs by Age: an ant nest and our home
activities.context: In many kinds of ants, a worker's job changes as she grows older. In this activity you compare ant jobs with the jobs people of different ages do at home.

materials.item: paper and a pencil

schedule.what: Make two lists of jobs by age, one for ants and one for your home, and compare.

activities.record: Two lists side by side: 'Ant jobs, young to old' and 'Home jobs, young to old'.

setup.art: A cut-away ant nest with young ants caring for eggs deep inside and older ants walking out of the entrance.
setup.caption: 1. Young ants work inside. Older ants go out.

setup.art: A paper with two columns: ant jobs and home jobs, each with arrows from young to old.
setup.caption: 2. Make two lists and compare them.

flow.do: Read this list to your child: young worker ants look after the eggs and young. Middle-aged workers clean and build the nest. The oldest workers guard the entrance and go out to find food.
flow.say: In many kinds of ants, the youngest workers stay safe deep in the nest. The oldest ones go out, where it is most dangerous. Why might that be?
flow.kid: Young ants look after the babies. Older ants build. The oldest go out for food. Why the oldest?

ask.q: Why might the oldest ants do the most dangerous job?
good: Because they have less life left to lose.
Because the young ones are kept safe to work longer.

flow.parent: Scientists think this is right: a colony loses less when an old forager dies than a young one. Not every kind of ant works this way.

flow.do: Make a list of jobs at home by age. Write what the youngest child, a parent, and an older relative or neighbour (if there is one) each do.
flow.say: Now let's do our home. Who does which jobs? Is it about age, about skill, or something else?
flow.kid: Now list jobs at home. What do you do? What do the grown-ups do? What does an older relative or neighbour do?
flow.parent: There is no right answer. The point is to notice that every society shares out its work somehow.

flow.do: Compare the two lists.
flow.say: What is the same about the ant nest and our home? What is different?
flow.kid: What is the same? What is different?

activities.title: Howl and Find: how a pack keeps together
activities.context: Wolves howl to find each other when they are apart. In this activity you try to find your family in the flat by sound alone.

materials.item: two or more people and two or three rooms

schedule.what: Hide in different rooms and find each other by howling.

activities.record: Write how many howls it took to find each person.

setup.art: A girl standing in a hallway with her hand cupped to her ear, listening.
setup.caption: 1. One person waits in the hall, the others hide in different rooms.

setup.art: A parent and child howling with their heads tilted back, in a small flat.
setup.caption: 2. Howl, listen, walk towards the answer.

flow.do: Explain the rules. One person is the lost wolf and waits in the hall. The others go into different rooms and stay quiet. The lost wolf howls, and each hiding person howls back once. The lost wolf walks towards the howls with eyes open, and finds everyone.
flow.say: Wolves who are apart howl, and their family howls back. Let's see if you can find us by howling.
flow.kid: You are the lost wolf. Howl. Listen for the howl back. Walk towards it.
flow.context: This is the first step of Howl and Find. Here you learn the rules.

flow.do: Play two or three rounds. Count the howls it takes to find each person.
flow.say: Howl, then listen. Which way did the answer come from?
flow.kid: Howl. Stop. Listen. Walk towards the howl. Count your howls.

flow.do: Talk about why howling helps a pack.
flow.say: Wild wolves can hear a howl from several kilometres away. Why would that help a family who hunts over a large area?
flow.kid: Why would a wolf family need to call each other?

good: To find each other when they are apart.
To tell other wolves to stay away.

flow.parent: Wolf howls also tell other packs that this area is taken. Keep the howling short if neighbours are close.

activities.title: Street Dog Watch from the window
activities.context: Street dogs in Indian cities often live in small groups. If you can see a street from a window or balcony, this activity lets you watch a dog society.

materials.item: a window or balcony with a view of a street, and a notebook

activities.safety: Watch from the window or balcony. Don't go close to dogs you don't know.

schedule.what: Watch street dogs for 15 minutes. Note which dogs stay together and what they do.

activities.record: Give each dog a name and draw who stays near whom.

setup.art: A child at a balcony railing looking down at three street dogs resting by a tea stall.
setup.caption: 1. Watch from a window or balcony.

setup.art: A notebook with three dog drawings joined by lines, labelled with made-up names.
setup.caption: 2. Draw who stays near whom.

flow.do: 1. Watch the dogs for 10 minutes. 2. Give each one a name by their colour or a mark. 3. Note which dogs lie close together and which walk together.
flow.say: Anindita Bhadra and her team at IISER Kolkata study street dogs like these. Let's watch them the way a scientist would.
flow.kid: Watch the dogs. Give each one a name. Who stays together?
flow.context: This is the first step of the street dog watch. You watch dogs and note who stays together.

flow.do: Draw a line between dogs who stayed close. Talk about what you saw.
flow.say: Do these dogs look like a group? What did they do together?
flow.kid: Draw lines between dogs who stayed close. Are they a group?
flow.parent: If you can't see any dogs, try crows or pigeons, or try again at a different time of day.

projects.title: The Ant Road Map: three days with our colony
projects.context: In this project you map where the ants in your home walk, and find out when they are busiest.

materials.item: a large sheet of paper for a map of your kitchen
a pencil and a clock
a few grains of sugar
a magnifying glass, if you have one

schedule.what: Draw a map of the kitchen. Mark every ant road you can find.
Count the ants crossing one spot for 1 minute in the morning and in the evening.
Follow a road back to where the ants go in. Mark the nest entrance on the map.

projects.record: The map, with roads drawn in, the morning and evening counts, and the nest entrance marked with a star.

setup.art: A child's map of a kitchen with the platform, sink and window, and wavy lines showing ant roads.
setup.caption: 1. Draw the kitchen and mark the ant roads.

setup.art: A finger pointing at a tiny crack under a tile where ants go in and out.
setup.caption: 2. Follow a road back and find the entrance.

flow.do: 1. Draw a map of the kitchen from above. 2. Look for lines of ants along the walls, the platform and the floor. 3. Draw each road on the map with a wavy line.
flow.say: Ant colonies have roads, like a city. Let's make a map of the ant roads in our kitchen.
flow.kid: Draw the kitchen from above. Find the ant lines. Draw each one on your map.
flow.parent: If you find no ants, leave a few grains of sugar near the window or a wall for an hour, then look again.
flow.context: This is the first day of the ant road map. You draw the kitchen and mark where ants walk.

flow.do: Pick one spot on a road. Count the ants crossing it in 1 minute, in the morning and again in the evening.
flow.say: When are the ants busiest? Let's count at the same spot, morning and evening.
flow.kid: Pick one spot. Count the ants that cross it in 1 minute. Do it again tonight.
flow.wait: Count once in the morning and once in the evening.

flow.do: 1. Follow one road back, away from any food, to where the ants go into a crack or a hole. 2. Mark it on the map with a star. 3. Talk about what might be inside.
flow.say: Somewhere behind that crack is the nest, with the queen and the young. We won't open it. Let's mark it on our map.
flow.kid: Follow the ants back. Where do they go in? Mark it with a star. Don't poke it!

check.q: Where is the queen of these ants, most likely?
options: Walking at the front of the line
Deep inside the nest, laying eggs
At the food, telling the others to carry it
check.why: The queen stays deep inside the nest, laying eggs. The ants on the road are workers, her daughters. Picking 'at the front of the line' is a natural guess if you think a queen must lead. But no ant leads the line.

challenges.title: A Living Bridge
challenges.context: Army ants hook their own bodies together to make bridges, so the rest of the colony can cross a gap. In this challenge you build a bridge from many small parts.
challenges.problem: Build a bridge across a 20 cm gap between two piles of books, using many small parts joined together. The bridge must hold a one-rupee coin in the middle.
constraints: Use only small parts: paper clips, strips of paper, or rubber bands.
No single part may be longer than 5 cm.
You may not use tape across the gap. Tape may hold only the ends on the books.
materials: strips of newspaper about 5 cm long
two piles of books, each about 15 cm high, the same height
general: Hook paper clips into long chains and lay several chains side by side, like a rope bridge.
Fold paper strips into loops and link them like a paper chain.
Twist two chains together so they share the weight.
creative: Weaver ants hold leaves together with their bodies while their sisters glue them. Can you weave paper strips over and under your chains to make a deck?
Make the bridge sag in a curve, like a hammock, so each part pulls on its neighbours.
Build an arch from folded paper loops pushing against each other.
challenges.your_turn: Now design your own bridge from small parts. Draw it, build it and test it with one coin, then two. How many coins can it hold?

flow.do: 1. Make two piles of books, each about 15 cm high and the same height. 2. Put them 20 cm apart. 3. Show your child a picture of army ants making a bridge, if you can find one.
flow.say: Army ants in the rainforests of Central and South America hook their legs together to make bridges with their own bodies. No ant is in charge of building the bridge. Can we build a bridge from small parts?
flow.kid: Set the books 20 cm apart. Ants build bridges out of their bodies. Can you build one from small parts?
flow.context: This is the first step of the Living Bridge challenge. Here you set up the gap.

flow.do: Draw three ideas before building.
flow.say: Let's draw three ideas first. Which one do you think will hold the coin, and why?
flow.kid: Draw three ideas. Which one will hold the coin? Why?

flow.do: 1. Build the best idea. 2. Put a coin in the middle. 3. If it falls, find the weak spot and fix it. 4. Add a second coin.
flow.say: Test it. If it breaks, where did it break? How can the parts share the weight better?
flow.kid: Build it. Put the coin on. Did it hold? Fix the weak spot. Try two coins.

flow.do: Talk about what worked.
flow.say: What made the strongest bridge? How is that like ants holding on to each other?
flow.kid: What made it strong? How is it like the ants?

ask.q: Why can many small parts hold more than one part alone?
good: Because they share the weight.
Because each part holds on to its neighbours.
