opts: Any crowd of animals in one place
A group of animals of one kind who live together for a long time and help each other
quiz.why: A society's members stay together, know each other and share the work. A crowd of pigeons at a grain shop is not a society: they just happen to be in one place.

quiz.p: Why is an old matriarch useful to her family in a drought?
opts: She may remember where water was in a drought long ago
quiz.why: Her long memory is the family's store of knowledge. Strength and speed don't find hidden water.

quiz.p: Where do adult male elephants usually live?
opts: As the leaders of the families
Alone, or in loose groups of males
In the middle of the family, guarding the calves
quiz.why: Males leave their family as teenagers and live apart, visiting families only for a short time.

quiz.p: In many kinds of ants, which workers go out of the nest to look for food?
quiz.why: In many kinds of ants, young workers stay safe inside the nest and the older workers go out to forage. The queen stays deep in the nest.

quiz.p: How does an ant tell her sisters where food is?
opts: By leaving a scent trail, made of pheromone, on the way home
By carrying every sister to the food
quiz.why: She dabs pheromone on the floor as she walks home. Other ants follow the smell.

quiz.p: Priya, a girl in Class 3 in Hyderabad, put a weak and a strong sugar drop near an ant road. After 30 minutes the strong drop had 20 ants and the weak drop had 3. What is the best explanation?
opts: The ants at the strong drop were bigger
Ants that drank the strong sugar laid more scent, so more ants followed their trail
The queen chose the strong drop
quiz.why: A sweeter food makes ants lay more trail scent, so the trail grows stronger and pulls in more ants. No ant gave orders.

quiz.p: In a sugar drop test, why should both drops be the same distance from the ant road?
opts: So that only the sweetness is different, and neither drop gets an unfair start
Because ants can only see a short way
quiz.why: In a fair test you change only one thing. If one drop is closer, ants may find it first, and then you can't tell whether sweetness or distance made the difference.

quiz.p: Who leads a wild wolf pack, usually?
opts: The parents: a mother and a father
quiz.why: A wild pack is a family, so the parents lead and the young follow, as children follow parents.

quiz.p: Where did the idea of a fighting 'alpha wolf' come from?
opts: From watching wild wolf families for many years
From watching strangers put together in a zoo
quiz.why: Rudolph Schenkel watched unrelated wolves in a zoo in Basel in the 1940s. They fought for rank. David Mech later watched wild wolves and showed that packs are families.

opts: To find each other when apart, and to tell other packs to keep away
quiz.why: A howl carries far. Pack members use it to find each other, and other packs hear that the area is taken. The full moon has nothing to do with it.

quiz.p: In what way is a human family most like an elephant family?
opts: Children learn a lot from older relatives, such as grandmothers
quiz.why: In both, the young learn from older family members. In many human families sons stay, so that part is different.

quiz.p: Which of these do scientists still argue about?
opts: Whether an ant colony is one mind, a superorganism
quiz.why: The other three are settled by long study. Whether a colony is one being or many ants following rules is still debated.

items.p: Who leads an elephant family?
opts: The biggest male, with the longest tusks
The oldest female, called the matriarch
items.why: An elephant family is led by the matriarch, usually the oldest female. Adult males live apart. A strong answer adds why: she remembers the most.

items.p: Every worker ant you see on the kitchen platform is a female.
items.why: True. Worker ants are all females, daughters of the queen. Male ants hatch only at certain times of year, have wings, and live a short time.

items.p: An ant smells, tastes and touches with the two feelers on her head, called ____.
items.why: Ants use their antennae to follow a trail and to tap each other when they meet.

items.p: Match each society to who leads it.
items.a: pairs as given
items.why: An elephant family follows the matriarch. A wolf pack follows the parents. In an ant colony, the queen lays eggs but does not lead, and the ants decide together.

items.p: Sort these animals of an elephant family: who stays with the family all their life, and who will leave?
items.a: see items
items.why: Female elephants stay with their mothers and grandmother all their lives. Males leave as teenagers and live alone or with other males. The 13-year-old son will probably leave soon.

items.p: Why does an elephant family follow the oldest female, and not the biggest one? Give one reason.
items.a: Because she has lived the longest, so she remembers the most: where to find water in a dry year, the safe paths and which dangers are real.
items.why: A strong answer links age to memory and experience, and gives an example such as finding water in a drought.

items.p: Meenakshi, a girl in Class 3 in Coimbatore, wipes a short piece of an ant road with a wet cloth. What do the ants arriving at the wiped part probably do?
opts: Stop and wander about, then find the trail again
Turn round and go home for ever
items.why: Wiping removes the pheromone scent. The ants lose the trail, wander, and soon find the scent again on the other side, or lay new scent. This shows that ants follow the smell, not each other's eyes.

items.p: Draw an ant nest cut open. Show the queen, eggs, young workers caring for the eggs, and older workers going out.
items.a: A nest with a queen deep inside, eggs near her, young workers next to the eggs, and older workers near the entrance and outside.
items.why: A strong drawing shows the queen deep in the nest and the older ants outside, because in many kinds of ants the oldest workers forage.
items.art: A blank outline of a nest underground, with an entrance at the top.

items.p: The queen ant walks out of the nest and tells the workers where the food is.
items.why: False. The queen stays deep inside the nest and lays eggs. She gives no orders. Workers find food and share the news with scent trails.

items.p: Put in order how a line of ants forms at a sugar drop.
items: Many ants follow the trail, and lay more scent
She lays scent on her way back to the nest
Other ants smell the trail and follow it out
a: She lays scent on her way back to the nest
Other ants smell the trail and follow it out
Many ants follow the trail, and lay more scent
items.why: The first ant finds the food, then marks the way home. Others follow the scent, and add their own, so the trail grows stronger and more ants come.

items.p: In the wild, young wolves usually stay in their parents' pack for the rest of their lives.
items.why: False. Most young wolves leave when they are grown, to find a mate and start a pack of their own.

items.p: A large group of ants living together in one nest is called a ____.
items.why: A colony is a large group of insects of one kind living together in one nest. Ants, termites and honeybees live in colonies.

items.p: Label the ant: head, antennae, legs, and the part at the back called the abdomen, where she makes the trail scent.
items.a: Head with two antennae at the front, six legs on the middle part, and the abdomen at the back.
items.why: Ants smell with their antennae and make trail pheromone in glands, most often in the abdomen. A strong answer labels all six legs on the middle part, the thorax.
items.art: An outline drawing of an ant seen from above, with four empty label lines.

items.p: In your sugar drop test, how did you know when ants were following a trail, and not just wandering?
items.a: The ants walked one behind another along the same path between the drop and the ant road, and the line got busier.
items.why: A strong answer uses evidence from the test: ants walking in a line, on the same path, in both directions, and more ants over time.

items.p: Two friends in Kochi watch a long line of ants carrying rice grains.

views.says: There must be a leader ant at the front, showing the others the way.
There is no leader. Every ant just follows the smell.

items.ask: Who do you agree with? Use what you saw in your ant watch or sugar test. Then say one thing the other friend has right.
items.a: A strong answer agrees with Farhan, using evidence: no ant was in charge, and ants followed the scent trail. It also gives Anjali some credit: one ant did find the food first, so the first ant did show the way, by leaving scent.
items.why: The first ant does lead in a way, by laying the first trail, but she gives no orders and the line keeps going without her. A strong answer sees both.

items.p: In Amboseli, scientists played lion roars to elephant families. Which families reacted most strongly to the roars of male lions?
opts: Families with a very old matriarch
items.why: Old matriarchs reacted most to male lions, who are the most dangerous to calves. They had learned over a long life which roars mean the most danger.

items.p: A drought comes that happens only once in 30 years. Why might a family with a 60-year-old matriarch do better than a family with a 25-year-old one?
items.a: The 60-year-old has lived through a drought like this before, and may remember where water was. The 25-year-old has never seen one.
items.why: A strong answer links the matriarch's age to having lived through an earlier drought, as in the 1993 drought in Tanzania.

items.p: Sort these into what one ant does and what the whole colony does.
items: ends up mostly at the sweeter drop
lays scent on her way home
builds a road from the nest to the food
moves house when the nest floods
items.a: see items
items.why: Each ant makes small choices. Added together, these become choices of the whole colony, such as where most ants go or when to move house.

items.p: If ants find a weak sugar drop first and build a strong trail to it, they may keep going there even after a sweeter drop is put out.
items.why: True. Scientists have seen this in the lab. A strong trail keeps drawing ants, so the colony can get stuck on the first food it found. Group choices are good, but not perfect.

items.p: How can an ant tell a sister from an ant of another colony?
opts: By her smell, which she checks with her antennae
By the colour of her legs
items.why: Ants of one colony share a smell on their bodies. An ant touches a stranger with her antennae and smells that she is not from her nest.

items.p: Draw a graph of your sugar drop test: minutes along the bottom, number of ants up the side, with one line for each drop.
items.a: Two lines, both starting near zero. The strong-drop line rises faster and higher. The weak-drop line stays low.
items.why: A strong drawing labels both axes, both lines, and shows the strong drop gaining ants faster as more ants laid scent.

items.p: A group of wolves who live and hunt together is called a ____.
items.why: A wild wolf pack is usually a family: a mother, a father and their young.

items.p: Three of these live in societies. Which one usually lives alone?
items.why: Adult tigers usually live and hunt alone, except mothers with cubs. Elephants, wolves and ants live in groups.

items.p: Match each scientist to what she studied.
pairs: elephant families in Amboseli, Kenya, since 1972
how harvester ants decide to go out for food
Asian elephant families at Kabini, Karnataka
items.a: pairs as given
items.why: These women have spent many years watching animal societies. Long watching is how we know what animals really do.

items.p: Two scientists argue about an ant colony.

views.says: The colony is like one big animal. It chooses as one, the way your body does.
The colony is many ants. Each ant chooses, and the colony's choice is just all of them added up.

items.ask: Which scientist do you agree with? Use your sugar drop test as evidence. Then give the best point the other scientist makes.
items.a: A strong answer uses the test: each ant laid scent and followed trails, which supports Dr Kavitha, yet the crowd ended up at the sweeter drop as one, which supports Dr Lakshmi. Both views fit some of the evidence.
items.why: Scientists really do argue about this. A strong answer uses evidence for both and does not pretend the question is settled.

items.p: A wolf alone rarely catches a big deer, but a pack often can. Give two reasons why hunting together helps.
items.a: They can chase in turns, so the deer gets tired first. They can surround the deer, so the deer cannot escape.
items.why: A strong answer gives two different ways that cooperation helps, such as taking turns, surrounding prey, or guarding the catch from other animals.

items.p: Older brothers and sisters in a wolf pack often bring food to the new pups. What does this show about the pack?
opts: It is a family that raises the young together
Only the parents care for pups
The older wolves want to be the alpha
items.why: Wolf packs raise their pups together. Older young wolves carry meat in their stomachs and bring it up for the pups.

items.p: Label this elephant family picture: matriarch, mother, calf, teenage male.
items.a: The old female at the front is the matriarch. A female with a small elephant under her is a mother and calf. A young male with small tusks at the back is the teenage male.
items.why: A strong answer finds the matriarch at the front and the young male at the edge, ready to leave.
items.art: An elephant family walking in a line: an old female in front, a mother with a calf, and a young male with small tusks at the back.

items.p: Put a male elephant's life in order.
items: He lives alone or with other males
He is born into his mother's family
He visits families for a short time to mate
As a teenager, he starts to wander away
a: He is born into his mother's family
As a teenager, he starts to wander away
He lives alone or with other males
He visits families for a short time to mate
items.why: Male elephants grow up in their mother's family, leave as teenagers, then live apart, visiting families only to mate.

items.p: Termites live in colonies with both a king and a queen.
items.why: True. Unlike ants, a termite colony has a king who stays with the queen. Both ant and termite colonies are families.

items.p: Your friend says, 'A group needs a boss, or it will fall apart.' Use ants to argue against this, then say one way a leader can help a group.
items.a: Ants have no boss, yet the colony finds the best food and builds roads, because each ant follows the trail and adds her own scent. But a leader with knowledge helps too, like an elephant matriarch who remembers water.
items.why: A strong answer uses evidence on both sides: the leaderless ant colony and the elephant family led by experience.

items.p: In some places, poachers kill the oldest females in elephant families. What problem might the families have later, in a drought?
opts: No one remembers where water was in past droughts
The males come back to lead
items.why: The old matriarch's memory is lost with her. Younger females may never have lived through a drought, so they may not know where to find water.

items.p: Design a better sugar test. How would you find out whether ants pick the strong drop because it is sweeter, or only because they found it first?
items.a: Put out the weak drop first and let a trail form. Then add the strong drop at the same distance. If the ants move to the strong drop, sweetness wins. If they stay, finding it first wins. Repeat with the order swapped.
items.why: A strong answer changes only the order the drops are found, keeps everything else the same, and repeats the test.

items.p: A family in Madurai argues about the old 'alpha wolf' idea.

views.says: Scientists got it wrong once, so we can't trust anything scientists say about wolves.
Scientists found their own mistake by watching wild wolves. That is why we can trust them more.
Both of you have a point. We should ask how each idea was tested.

items.ask: Whose view do you agree with most, and why? Then answer back from one of the other views.
items.a: A strong answer explains that science corrects itself when better evidence comes, as when David Mech watched wild wolves and changed his mind. It also takes the worry seriously: the wrong idea spread for decades, so asking how something was tested is wise.
items.why: This is a real question about trust in science. A strong answer weighs all three views.

items.p: In Ropalidia marginata, a paper wasp found across India, what happens when the calm queen is taken away?
opts: One worker becomes very aggressive for a while, then becomes the next calm queen
The biggest wasp kills the others
The wasps fly off to find the old queen
items.why: Raghavendra Gadagkar's team found that one worker becomes very aggressive for a short time, then calms down and starts laying eggs as the new queen. So a queen can keep her place without bullying.

items.p: Draw a cartoon strip in four boxes showing how an elephant calf learns the way to the river from her grandmother, and later shows her own calf.
items.a: Box 1: calf walks behind grandmother in a dry year. Box 2: they reach the river. Box 3: years later, the calf is grown and leading. Box 4: she leads her own calf to the river.
items.why: A strong strip shows knowledge passing down the female line over many years.
items.art: Four empty boxes in a row.

items.p: Sort these into what helps a group and what is a cost of living in a group.
items: you can hunt bigger prey together
young ones can learn from old ones
you may have to wait for others
items.a: see items
items.why: Group life has costs as well as gains. Animals live in groups where the gains are bigger than the costs.

items.p: Kristen Hawkes found that Hadza grandmothers in Tanzania gather food that helps their grandchildren grow. How is this like an elephant matriarch, and how are the two different?
items.a: Alike: in both, an old female helps the young of her family survive. Different: the Hadza grandmother helps with food, and the matriarch mostly with knowledge and leading. People bring food to children by hand. Elephant calves drink their mother's milk, and learn from the family which plants to eat.
items.why: A strong answer gives one way they are alike and one way they differ, with a clear reason.

items.p: When many animals each make small choices, and together these become one choice for the group, scientists call it collective ____-making.
items.why: Collective decision-making is how ant colonies, honeybee swarms and flocks of birds choose together without a boss.

items.p: Honeybees choosing a new home send out scouts, who dance for the places they found. How does the swarm choose?
opts: The best place gets more and more dancers, until most scouts agree
They pick the first place found, always
items.why: Scouts dance longer for better places. More bees go to look, and dance too. The best place gains dancers fastest, like your strong sugar drop gaining ants.

items.p: On a sketch of your kitchen, label where you think the ant nest is, where the food is, and draw the trail between them.
items.a: A nest entrance at a crack or wall, a food spot such as the dustbin or sugar tin, and a line joining them.
items.why: A strong answer uses what the child saw, such as where ants disappeared into the wall.
items.art: A simple kitchen outline from above, with a platform, sink and window.

items.p: A tiger who lives alone has a smaller mind than an elephant who lives in a family.
items.why: False. Living alone is a way of life, not a smaller mind. Tigers sense, remember and decide for themselves all the time. Their food, large prey hunted by stealth, is easier to catch alone.

items.p: Match each message to the way the animal sends the message.
pairs: a scent trail on the floor
items.a: pairs as given
items.why: Each society uses the signals that suit their bodies and their world: smell for ants, sound for wolves and elephants, movement for bees.

items.p: Which of these is not led by its oldest female?
items.why: A wolf pack is led by both parents. Elephant families and killer whale families are led by old females.

items.p: Scientists estimate that about 20 million billion ants are alive on Earth. Why do you think living in colonies has helped ants do so well?
items.a: Because thousands of sisters share the work, find food fast, defend the nest and raise the young together. One ant alone could do far less.
items.why: A strong answer links colony life to success: sharing jobs, fast recruitment to food, and defence.

applications: Elephant corridors, safe paths between forests, are kept open in India because elephant families use the same routes year after year.
Wildlife workers try hard to protect old matriarchs from poachers, because whole families depend on their memory.
Computer scientists copy ant trails to find short routes for delivery vans and for data on the internet. This is called ant colony optimisation.
Engineers build groups of small robots that work together with no leader, copying ants and bees.
Dog trainers have moved away from 'be the alpha' training, because wolf packs turned out to be families.
Farmers in parts of Asia have used weaver ants to guard fruit trees from pests for hundreds of years.

open_questions.q: Is an ant colony one mind, or many minds working together?
open_questions.why_open: Each ant senses and chooses, and the colony also makes choices. Scientists disagree on whether to call the colony a superorganism.

open_questions.q: How does an old matriarch store a memory of water from 35 years ago?
open_questions.why_open: Elephants have large brains with a big area for memory, but nobody knows how such long memories of places are kept.

open_questions.q: Do Asian elephant families work the same way as African ones?
open_questions.why_open: Most studies are of African savanna elephants. Studies at Kabini and in Sri Lanka show Asian families split and join more often, but much is still unknown.

open_questions.q: How does a colony of thousands of ants decide to move house?
open_questions.why_open: Scientists understand this well in a few kinds of ants, but there are more than 14,000 known kinds, and most have never been studied.

open_questions.q: Are Indian wolves a separate kind of wolf?
open_questions.why_open: Gene studies suggest that wolves in India are one of the oldest wolf lineages. Scientists still argue about whether they are a separate species.

ask_kids: Who is the oldest person you know? What do they remember that nobody else does?
Are the ants out today? Which way are they walking?
If our family were an elephant family, who would be the matriarch?
Who decides where people walk on a crowded platform or market?
Why do you think the oldest ants go out for food, and the young ones stay in the nest?
Have you ever heard street dogs howl together? Why might they do it?
What would be hard about living all alone, with no family or friends?
Do you think a crowd of people can make a good choice without a leader? When?

jokes.j: Why do ants never get sick?
Why is an elephant grandmother good at finding water?
jokes.a: She has been there before, and elephants remember.

jokes.j: Why don't ants ever get lost?
jokes.a: They always follow their nose. Well, their antennae.

jokes.j: Why did the wolf pups love dinner time?
jokes.a: Their big sister always brought it home.

jokes.j: What is an elephant's favourite way to phone home?
Why did the ant cross the kitchen platform?
jokes.a: To get to the sugar side.

jokes.j: What is a wolf's favourite kind of music?
Why did the elephant matriarch not need a map?
How many ants does it take to carry a laddu?
jokes.a: Just one to find it, and a hundred to finish it.

maths.problem: In a sugar drop test, after 30 minutes there were 22 ants on the strong drop and 4 ants on the weak drop. How many more ants were on the strong drop?
maths.explain: 22 ants on the strong drop take away 4 on the weak drop is 18. Check: 4 + 18 = 22.
maths.context: This is about the sugar drop test, where you counted ants on a weak and a strong sugar drop every 5 minutes.
maths.why_maths: Taking one count from the other shows how big the difference is, so we can see whether the colony really chose.

maths.problem: At a new sugar drop, Kavya, a girl in Class 3, counted 1 ant at 2 minutes, 2 ants at 4 minutes, 4 ants at 6 minutes and 8 ants at 8 minutes. If the pattern carries on, how many ants will there be at 10 minutes? Why might the pattern stop later?
maths.answer: 16 ants. Later the pattern stops because the drop gets crowded and runs out, and there are only so many ants in the colony.
maths.explain: Each count is double the one before: 1, 2, 4, 8. Double 8 is 16. Every ant that drank laid scent and brought more ants, so the number grew faster and faster. But no drop can feed endless ants, so the growth slows down.
maths.context: These are made-up counts from the first few minutes of a sugar drop test.
maths.why_maths: Spotting the doubling pattern explains why a trail grows so fast: each ant who drinks brings more ants.

maths.problem: An elephant mother carries her calf inside her for about 22 months before the calf is born. A human mother carries her baby for about 9 months. How many months longer is the elephant's wait?
maths.explain: 22 take away 9 is 13. So an elephant mother waits about 13 months more, more than a whole extra year.
maths.context: This is about elephant calves. Elephants wait longer for a baby than any other land animal.
maths.why_maths: Comparing the two numbers shows how much an elephant family invests in each calf, which is one reason they guard calves so carefully.

maths.problem: A wolf pack has 8 wolves: a mother, a father, 2 young wolves from last year and 4 new pups. What fraction of the pack are new pups?
maths.explain: There are 4 pups out of 8 wolves. 4 is half of 8. So half the pack are pups who need feeding.
maths.context: This is about a made-up wolf pack, built the way real wild packs are.
maths.why_maths: Knowing that half the pack can't hunt yet shows why the parents and older young wolves must bring food back for everyone.

maths.problem: In the Ask the Elders test, Nila's grandmother scored 5 out of 6, her mother scored 4, and Nila scored 3. Nila scored 3 out of 3 on the 'now' questions, and her grandmother scored 2 out of 3 on them. Who knew most about long ago, and who knew most about now?
maths.answer: The grandmother knew most about long ago: 3 out of 3. Nila knew most about now: 3 out of 3.
maths.explain: The grandmother's total was 5, and 2 of those were 'now' questions, so 5 - 2 = 3 were 'long ago'. Nila's total was 3, all 'now'. So each person knew most about the years they had lived through.
maths.context: This is about the Ask the Elders test, where you ask people of different ages the same 6 questions.
maths.why_maths: The total alone says the grandmother knows most. Splitting it into two parts shows a truer picture: knowledge depends on what each person lived through.

roots.context: We have learned how elephant families, ant colonies and wolf packs live and decide together. Now we ask what animal societies tell us about ourselves and the world.

deep_truth.truth: Usually the strong sugar drop ends up with far more ants than the weak one. No ant is in charge, and none gives orders. Ants that drink the sweeter sugar lay more scent on their way home. Those many small choices add up to one choice for the whole nest.
deep_truth.habit: We expect every group to have a boss who decides, like a captain or a head teacher. An ant nest has a queen, but she stays inside laying eggs and gives no orders. The choice is made by many ants together.
deep_truth.evidence: In the sugar drop test, the strong drop usually gains ants faster and faster, while the weak drop keeps only a few. The queen is never there. The ants decide out on the floor, one ant at a time.

three.who_am_i: You were born into a family, and you learned most of what you know from older people in it, just as an elephant calf learns from her grandmother.
three.what_is_life: Many living beings survive by living together. An elephant calf, a worker ant and a wolf pup could not grow up alone.
three.what_is_this_world: Scientists estimate that about 20 million billion ants are alive on Earth. All ants live in colonies, on nearly every piece of land.

roots.thread: One ant alone can find a drop of sugar. Thousands of ants, each sensing and choosing, find the best food and build roads to it. An elephant family carries the memory of their oldest member to every calf. In each society, the members act together, and each member still senses and chooses for herself.

teachings.teaching: Whatever a great person does, others do too. The example they set, the world follows.
teachings.link: An elephant family follows the matriarch because of what she does: where she walks, where she digs, when she stops to listen. She leads by example, not by orders.

teachings.teaching: The best leaders are hardly noticed. When the work is done, the people say, 'We did it ourselves.'
teachings.link: In your sugar test no ant was seen leading, yet the colony chose the sweeter drop. The choice came from the ants themselves.

teachings.source: Ubuntu, a teaching of the Nguni-speaking peoples of southern Africa: umuntu ngumuntu ngabantu
teachings.teaching: A person is a person through other people.
teachings.link: A worker ant, an elephant calf and a wolf pup each grow up through their family. What each one becomes depends on the others around them.

science.text: In lab tests, ant colonies end up mostly at the sweeter of two sugar drops, because ants lay more trail scent for sweeter food.
Whether a colony has a mind of its own, as well as each ant, is still argued about.

other_view.view: A colony is many ants following simple rules, such as 'lay more scent for sweeter food'. Calling the colony's choice a decision is a handy way of talking. It does not show that the colony is one being with a mind of its own.

practice.title: Walk without a leader
practice.say: Let's all stand up in the middle of the room. Nobody leads, and nobody talks. Each of us watches only the person next to us. If they move, we move a little the same way. Let's walk slowly for one minute. Now stop. Close your eyes and take five slow breaths. Did we move together? Who decided where we went?
practice.kid: Stand with your family. Nobody talks. Watch the person next to you. Move when they move. Now stop. Breathe slowly five times. Who decided where you went?

how_we_found_out.story: In the 1940s, a Swiss scientist called Rudolph Schenkel watched wolves in a zoo in Basel. The wolves were strangers who had been put together in one enclosure. They fought often. Schenkel wrote that a top male and a top female, which he called the 'alpha' wolves, won their place by fighting. In 1970, the American scientist David Mech used the word in a popular book, The Wolf. Soon people everywhere believed that a wolf pack is ruled by the toughest fighter. Then Mech spent many summers on Ellesmere Island, in the far north of Canada, watching wild wolves who had little fear of people. He saw that a wild pack is a family: a mother, a father and their young from the last few years. The 'alpha' pair were simply the parents. The young wolves followed them as children follow their parents, and fights were rare. In 1999 Mech published what he had found. He asked his publisher to stop printing his old book. Scientists now think the zoo wolves fought because they were strangers forced together, not a family.
how_we_found_out.who: Rudolph Schenkel, a Swiss animal scientist, and L. David Mech, an American wolf scientist
how_we_found_out.when: 1947 (Schenkel's zoo study), 1970 (Mech's book The Wolf), 1999 (Mech's paper on wild wolves)
how_we_found_out.wrong_idea: People thought a wolf pack was ruled by an 'alpha' wolf who fought his way to the top. Watching wild wolves for many years showed that a pack is a family, and the so-called alphas are the parents.
